19703-madame-delphine:
George W. Cable wrote about Creole New Orleans with unmatched local knowledge. Madame Delphine is one of his best-known stories of that city. Its opening shows a quarter sunk into long decay. Old commercial glory has shrunk into small shops. Bright market stalls stand out like patches of mould. Cable sets mood before he sets plot in motion.

Cable's New Orleans tales deal with caste, color, and old French families. Madame Delphine stands at the center of such a tale. Her story turns on sacrifice within a rigid social order. Cable wrote the city's speech and streets from life. His work helped define Southern local-color fiction. This short novel remains a fine place to meet it.
19779-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-20-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1867 is volume 20, number 118 of the magazine. One essay here treats grief with striking practicality. Grief, it says, must be fed with thought or starve to death. The best plan is keeping the mind busy with other work. The essay calls busyness a spiritual anesthetic for sorrow. Such counsel filled postwar American magazines.

The Civil War had ended two years before this issue. Its readers knew bereavement at national scale. The Atlantic mixed essays, fiction, and reviews for educated households. A single issue preserves the era's whole mental diet. Scholars read such numbers to hear 1867 thinking aloud. This one speaks in a Boston accent, thoughtful and composed.
19939-history-of-the-missions-of-the-ame:
This history covers missions of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Its ground is the Ottoman world: Armenians, Greeks, and the Turkish empire. In March 1846, Sir Stratford Canning reported from Constantinople. Thirty-six evangelical Armenians stood persecuted by their Patriarch, he wrote. Canning added personal efforts to soften their treatment. Diplomacy and missions intertwine through the narrative.

The American Board sent its first missionaries abroad in 1812. Its Near East missions built schools, presses, and colleges. Armenian converts stood at the center of this volume's story. Persecution reports shaped American sympathy and policy. The history is both record and advocacy. Scholars of missions still work through its documents.
19941-with-our-army-in-palestine:
John Morecroft wrote With Our Army in Palestine about the British campaign there. He corrects the home public's short version of that war. Most people think the Great Crusade began with taking Jerusalem, he says. They think it ended when the Turks surrendered in autumn 1918. That view is entirely erroneous, he insists. The campaign was longer, wider, and harder than the famous dates suggest.

Palestine saw fighting from Gaza to Damascus over two years. Allenby's army mixed British, Indian, Australian, and Arab forces. Morecroft marched with them as an official observer and writer. His book restores the campaign's full length. Desert, water, and distance are its real antagonists. It is solid campaign history from a participant.
19996-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for October 1865 is volume 16, number 96. The Civil War had ended six months before this issue. One article attacks a fashionable claim about American health. Physical decay, it is said, threatens the American people. Unwise stimulation of the brain gets the blame. A deficiency of physical health in America is assumed as an axiom. The writer questions that assumption sharply. Postwar nerves were a national topic that autumn.

The magazine now spoke for a victorious, grieving Union. Its pages balanced reconstruction politics with science and letters. Health anxiety ran through much postwar writing. This article shows the argument in its first form. A single number captures the culture re-sorting itself. Scholars still read these volumes as America's diary.
20071-sue-a-little-heroine:
L. T. Meade wrote Sue, A Little Heroine, one of her many books for young readers. Sue is a small girl with a freckled face and red-tinged hair. Her eyes are bright blue and keen, the book notes at once. She pushes through a crowd to hear a street preacher speak.

A rough man lays a hand on her shoulder in that crowd. From such small scenes, Meade builds a tale of a brave child. Sue faces hard city life with faith and pluck. Readers get a Victorian tale of poverty, courage, and a child's good heart under strain.
20263-boswell-s-correspondence-with-the-:
James Boswell's correspondence with Andrew Erskine appears here with notes by George Birkbeck Hill. Hill praises a young Scot who dared to tour Corsica's interior. No traveler from Britain had visited that interior before him. Turkish corsairs still swarmed the Mediterranean in that risky age.

Corsica itself sat in a very unsettled state at the time. Boswell's letters show his wit, ambition, and love of great men. Erskine, a poet and soldier, proved a bright partner in letters. Readers get lively eighteenth-century correspondence, richly framed by a top editor.
20340-a-little-maid-of-old-maine:
Alice Turner Curtis wrote A Little Maid of Old Maine, a tale of the Revolution. Two girls carry a big basket toward the Machias River in Maine. It is a pleasant May morning in 1775, full of pine scent. Freshly cut logs have been poled downriver to the big sawmills.

War news from Lexington has just reached the Maine coast that spring. Machias would soon fight one of the first naval battles of the war. Curtis sets her little maid amid lumber, ships, and patriots. Young readers get Maine's own Revolution story, told at a child's height.
20378-christmas-sunshine:
Christmas Sunshine is a seasonal gift book of verse and readings for the Christmas season. Its pages mix classic religious poetry with pieces on winter, snow, and the birth of Christ. The selection suits family reading by the fireside.

One passage praises winter as it hides the bare earth under innocent snow. It speaks of a saintly veil of maiden white thrown over the year's shame. Such lines show the book's mix of nature writing and devotion, and the warmth its makers hoped to bring into the home at Christmas.
20496-legends-of-the-rhine:
Legends of the Rhine brings the old tales of Germany's great river to English-speaking readers. Castles, knights, water spirits, and doomed lovers crowd its pages. The book mixes travel talk with the legends themselves, in the manner of a journey up the river.

One scene has a young woman smile at a compliment to her mother. The mother, it turns out, was English by birth. The traveler remarks that Germany is the land of romance for the English, just as Italy is for the Germans. The legends that follow show why the Rhine earned that name.
20513-how-to-succeed-or-stepping-stones-:
Orison Swett Marden's How to Succeed, published in 1896, is one of the founding books of the success movement. Its full title promises stepping stones to fame and fortune. Marden told young readers that will and character, not luck, make a life.

Do not look far for the successful man, he writes. This man is you, it is I, it is each one of us. How do we constitute ourselves men? Nothing is harder if we do not know how to will it, and nothing easier if we will it. Such bracing talk made Marden's books steady sellers.
20616-the-old-front-line:
John Masefield walked the Somme battlefield soon after the fighting and wrote The Old Front Line about what he found. Masefield had served in France and wrote with a poet's eye. The book describes the trenches, villages, and graves of the 1916 battle.

He looks ahead to peace. The ground full of death will grow food again, he writes, and this frontier of trouble will be forgotten. When the trenches are filled in and the plough has gone over them, the land will not long keep the look of war. The book became a classic of battlefield writing.
21027-the-trial-of-charles-random-de-ber:
False word of peace with France, spread to lift the funds, charges the Crown in this trial. Charles de Berenger, Lord Cochrane, and others stood accused of that fraud in 1814. The Trial records a plot to make the king and public believe peace was near.

Stock Exchange fraud, a fake colonel, and a staged ride from Dover fill the case. Cochrane, a sea hero, swore his innocence to his death's door. The verdict wrecked his career, though later ages cleared his name in part. Trial reports like this preserve court drama word for word, cross-talk, proof, and all.
21119-flaming-june:
A tidy elderly spinster in a seaside town keeps a large house. It has private access to a shared garden, and her settled life is upset by a visitor. Her brother, now rich in America, sends his daughter Cornelia to England as part of her education. Cornelia arrives with plenty of pocket money and American habits.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey sets the girl among polished, well-bred people who expect chaperones and strict manners. Cornelia gads about with young men as she pleases, to her aunt's dismay. The aunt proves right in the end: among all the nice people hides one bad character, revealed only near the close.
21250-sir-walter-scott-a-lecture-at-the-:
William Paton Ker delivered this lecture on Sir Walter Scott at the Sorbonne on May 22, 1919, in the Louis Liard series. He takes his text from Scott's own account of seeing Ivanhoe turned into an opera at the Odéon in Paris. Scott, who dictated much of that novel in pain at Abbotsford, marvelled that it now amused a foreign crowd.

Ker contrasts Scott's regional Scotland, its dialect barely clear outside its own ground, with the Europe-wide market that fought for his novels. The lecture first appeared in the Anglo-French Review in August 1919. It is a short, warm weighing of Scott's European fame.
21273-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-2-no-1:
The Atlantic Monthly for December 1858, volume two, number fourteen, opens with an essay on the ideal tendency in art. Its writer argues that art is the largest expression, pointing toward what cannot be measured or lodged in systems. Shakespeare, Plato, Michelangelo, Beethoven, and Goethe stand as its witnesses.

The young Atlantic, founded in Boston the year before, aimed to lead American letters, art, and politics in one magazine. A single monthly number like this one mixes essays, stories, poems, and reviews by the New England circle. Kept whole, it shows the magazine in its second year, when its table of contents was itself an argument about American culture.
21288-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1866, volume seventeen, number 101, leads with passages from Hawthorne's notebooks, published two years after his death. One entry describes a July 1837 drive near Augusta, Maine, to fish for white perch through a crooked, winding brook. The pilot talks politics and the bank between hearty tugs at a whiskey bottle.

Several dozen fish, yellow perch, a great chub, and horned pouts come home in an hour or two. Ticknor and Fields published the magazine in Boston as a monthly of literature, science, art, and politics. A single issue preserves its post-Civil War table, where Hawthorne's private journals shared space with the day's essays.
21325-outlines-of-greek-and-roman-medici:
James Sands Elliott was a New Zealand doctor and editor of the New Zealand Medical Journal. He wrote these outlines after a stay in southeastern Europe stirred his interest. Published in 1914, the book traces the main stages of healing in the Greek and Roman worlds. Those are the two empires to which modern civilisation owes most. Asklepios, the Greek god of healing, fronts it.

Elliott complains that the history of medicine is much neglected, even by doctors, so that many discoveries are only rediscoveries. He keeps the book a general outline rather than a full treatise, leaning on German historians like Baas and Sprengel. It serves as a short, readable first map of ancient medicine.
21408-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The April 1866 number of the Atlantic Monthly, volume seventeen, number one hundred and two, leads with the last days of Walter Savage Landor. Landor had died at Florence in September 1864, and many readers barely knew his name. The piece asks why so bright a writer was so little read.

The Atlantic was then a leading magazine of letters, science, art, and public life. Its pages mixed essays, reviews, poems, and tales for a broad, keen readership. This number preserves a slice of that world just after the Civil War. Emerson's own account of Landor, from English Traits, is quoted and weighed.
21572-percival-keene:
Percival Keene grows up near Southampton in Captain Marryat's novel of 1842, his nineteenth book. An old mansion house, known by its name for centuries, stands a few miles from the town. Sea service, in the channel frigate world of the day, shapes the hero's path.

Channel service, Marryat jokes, meant a captain with a seat in Parliament. His frigate rarely went to sea while the House was sitting, lest his vote be missed. Against that sly background, young Keene learns the navy as it truly was. Love, patronage, and action fill a tale told with Marryat's usual pace and humour.
21642-lady-cadogan-s-illustrated-games-o:
Lady Cadogan's Illustrated Games of Solitaire, in a new revised edition of 1914, adds American games. David McKay of Philadelphia issued the book, under the motto that patience conquers. A line from Othello asks how poor are they that have not patience.

Terms come first: foundation cards, suitable cards, and marriage, meaning a card placed on its neighbour in suit. Games run from Canfield, or Klondike, to Napoleon at St Helena and the Besieged City. La Belle Lucie, the Flower Garden, and the Sultan crowd the long contents list. Players get clear rules and pictures for dozens of single-player card games.
21716-the-battery-and-the-boiler-adventu:
A baby born at sea in a howling storm grows up to work with the newest wonder of his age in this Ballantyne tale. The boy's early squalls mark him, the ship's cook jokes, as one who will make his mark somehow. He finds his chance in the laying of submarine telegraph cables, the wires that first linked lands across the oceans.

Ballantyne studied cable laying firsthand, as he did for many of his books on trades and crafts. Storms, ships, sparks, and mishaps fill the story, mixing sea adventure with early electrical work. Readers get a lively look at the crews who strung the world's first ocean telegraph lines.
22058-cornelius-o-dowd-upon-men-and-wome:
Charles Lever, the Irish novelist, created Cornelius O'Dowd as a comic mask for his magazine essays. The pieces first ran in Blackwood's Magazine and were gathered in book form in 1864. O'Dowd introduces himself as a man who waited fourteen years at levees for government favour. No viceroy ever gave him a post, which leaves him free to talk.

From Italian battlefields to Dublin drawing rooms, O'Dowd comments on everything. Garibaldi's worshippers, Solferino, Italian law, and organ grinders all come under his eye. The humour is broad, Irish, and topical. Readers in the 1860s took these papers as light relief with a sting.
22090-the-task-of-social-hygiene:
Havelock Ellis, the English writer on sex and society, set out his programme in The Task of Social Hygiene. Ellis says social hygiene grows out of the older idea of social reform, but goes deeper. Reform treated bad conditions as they arose. Hygiene, as he defines it, aims at prevention: finding the source of social ills before they take hold.

Ellis discusses the family, birth, education, and the health of the race. Some of his views carry the stamp of his age's faith in eugenics, which readers now judge harshly. Others look ahead to public health and planned welfare. The book is a clear statement of how one Edwardian thinker hoped science would remake society.
22097-byeways-in-palestine:
James Finn served as British consul in Jerusalem through the middle of the nineteenth century. His Byeways in Palestine gathers journeys off the beaten road of the Holy Land. Finn admits he carried no fine instruments, only sometimes a common thermometer. He had no time for digging or surveying; his consular work came first.

What he offers instead is close knowledge of the country and its peoples. Fellahin villages, Bedouin camps, Samaritan and Jewish communities all appear. Finn notices crops, ruins, customs, and quarrels with a resident's eye. The book is a useful record of Ottoman Palestine before tourists and archaeologists remade the picture of it.
22245-steve-and-the-steam-engine:
Sara Ware Bassett wrote Steve and the Steam Engine in 1921, a boys' novel with a railroad heart. Steve begins the book in disgrace. While his parents were in New York and the chauffeur lay in hospital, he took the family's big six-cylinder car without permission. He carried a crowd of friends to a football game at Torrington, and that, the narrator warns, was not the worst of it.

To earn back trust, Steve is sent to work where steam engines rule. Bassett's Cape Cod tales usually smell of salt water; here coal smoke takes over. The book teaches railroad practice inside a story of a boy making good. It is wholesome series fiction of the post-war years.
22317-george-bowring-a-tale-of-cader-idr:
George Bowring is R. D. Blackmore's tale of Cader Idris, drawn from Slain by the Doones. Cader Idris is the great Welsh mountain of legend. The story, though, opens with school days and a sudden parting.

Within a week, George and the narrator were forced to leave their school. They left the grand old town and the lovely Severn too. All they kept was one another. That loss hangs over the tale from its first pages. Blackmore blends boyhood friendship with Welsh mountain country. Readers get a short, fond, sorrowful story from a writer best known for the wilder Doone country nearby.
22470-the-bell-tone:
Edmund H. Leftwich wrote The Bell Tone, a science fiction story of alien signals. Its narrator studies a wave used for sending thought images. The wave measures .00176 meter, he reports with care.

Pictures may be sent with a clacking code or independently. The narrator can conceive no finer communications system than this. He resolves that he must learn their secret methods fully. That hunger to decode drives the tale's investigation of contact. Thought pictures cross space by tone in his account. Readers get an inventor's-eye tale of first contact by signal. It prizes clever decoding over battles or chases in space.
22511-rollo-on-the-rhine:
Jacob Abbott wrote Rollo on the Rhine for his famous Rollo travel series. Rollo tours Europe with his family, learning geography as he goes. This volume follows the great Rhine river country of Germany.

Abbott first explains how mountain waters find the sea. Thousands of smaller torrents unite into larger and larger streams. At length they make four mighty rivers of Europe. Streams of the southern slopes form one great river, the Po. It flows east into the Adriatic Sea, he teaches. Such lessons precede the castles and towns of the Rhine itself. Young readers learned Europe's rivers through a boy's journey. Abbott's calm, instructive voice made the series a household standard.
22833-alcyone:
Vast, empty space opens Alcyone, a long poem named for a bright star. Its opening crosses a lifeless waste where night rules alone, vast and still. Nothing lives there now. Only the crumbled remains of ancient worlds lie scattered through the silence.

From that cosmic graveyard the poem ranges over time, death, and the fate of worlds. Its manner is grand and solemn, closer to meditation than to story. Readers should expect sweeping questions rather than characters. The verse belongs to a period when astronomy fed poetry, and new knowledge of deep space stirred awe as much as fear. Alcyone preserves that awe in period dress.
23005-eli-first-published-in-the-century:
A boat needs painting in Eli, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. A boy comes down to the shore, and his father rises, surveying the green bottom of the boat. Mother sent word that dinner is ready, the father guesses. He must eat fast, he says, and finish painting the boat's far side before the tide turns.

Tide rules everything in Chaplin's fishing world, even dinner. His Eli is built from such small, true pressures, work against water, hunger against duty. The dialect stays light on the page and exact to the ear. Stories like this one made his name in the great magazines. They preserve the speech and labor of the New England shore, net by net and coat of paint by coat.
23006-five-hundred-dollars-first-publish:
Captains swap a story in Five Hundred Dollars, Heman White Chaplin's tale first published in the Century Magazine. Captain Bennett opens the yarn by recalling David Prince's whaling voyage on the Viola. Captain Philo agrees that Prince's departure, at the time, looked suspiciously hurried. With most anyone else, he'd have thought something was up.

Whaling money and a hurried departure promise the rest. Chaplin lets two old sailors unfold the tale at harbor pace, hint by hint. Five hundred dollars, the title's sum, hangs over Prince's voyage from the first exchange. The frame is half the pleasure, gnarled narrators weighing a younger man's luck. It is a yarn in the true sense, spun dockside.
23007-the-village-convict-first-publishe:
Snow crunches at the store door in The Village Convict, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. Trade's looking up, William, Captain Seth tells the storekeeper, as someone kicks snow off his boots on the doorstep. Somebody's found he's got to have a shoestring before morning, he jokes.

Inside that warm store waits the village's judgment on a man marked by prison. Chaplin's convict returns to a place where everyone knows his record and measures his worth by his work. The story asks how much mercy a small town keeps in stock. Its setting does quiet argument, neighbors talking a man's fate over in the ordinary run of trade. Chaplin handles the question without preaching.
23040-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1866 argues about reunion. One essay imagines a statesman nearly despairing of the South after four years of war. Can anything good come from that quarter, he wonders. Yet a small, bright spot now shows at the Carolina cloud's very edge.

Hope and suspicion share this number, as they shared the country. Around the political essays sit poems, fiction, and reviews from the magazine's strong bench. The Atlantic stood at the center of American letters, and a monthly number shows its range in a single binding. August 1866 catches the nation mid-argument about what the war had settled. The spider's golden and silver silk of one image becomes, hopefully, a bond of union.
23108-chester-rand-or-the-new-path-to-fo:
Silas Tripp keeps the store in Chester Rand, or The New Path to Fortune. Silas Tripp may be Wyncombe's best-known citizen, the narrator figures. He runs the store in that Pennsylvania mountain village, lodges travelers in three spare rooms, serves as town treasurer, and fills other local offices besides.

Against Tripp's settled standing, young Chester Rand must find his path. Horatio Alger wrote this tale of a boy's rise, and its machinery is his, a good lad, a rich man to impress, luck that rewards virtue exactly on schedule. Store, town office, and mountain town fill the stage. Readers get the Alger formula in working order, cheerful, moral, and sure that fortune favors the deserving.
23137-diary-in-america-series-one:
Travelers contradict each other in Diary in America, series one. Talented travelers described the same nation in wildly clashing ways, the diarist marvels. Their harvests of fact, he adds, were generally meager for all their talent. The judgments pronounced on America, and pronounced so unjust by Americans, excited his curiosity.

Captain Frederick Marryat, the naval novelist, crossed the Atlantic to see for himself in the late 1830s. His diary records steamboats, prisons, elections, and manners with a sailor's bluntness. America fascinated and exasperated him by turns. Marryat's diary stands among the sharpest of the many British travel books on the young republic. Its author sized up a whole country with a naval officer's eye.
a-florentine-tragedy-la-sainte-courtisan: Wilde's unfinished verse dramas: A Florentine Tragedy, a bloody Renaissance tale of adultery and murder, and La Sainte Courtisane, his fragment about a courtesan and a hermit. Both show Wilde reaching for a grander, darker stage. Fascinating ruins from a genius cut short.
a-rebellious-heroine: John Kendrick Bangs's Rebellious Heroine: a novel's heroine rebels. The comic fantasy of fiction come alive. Droll and clever. Bangs's metafiction, bangs's heroine rebels against her author, droll metafiction, clever and funny, Bangs's fancy, metafiction.
a-ride-across-palestine: A Ride Across Palestine records a Victorian tour of the Holy Land. The keen traveler rides through deserts and old towns on horseback, notebook in hand. Holy places and local ways of life come alive together. A vivid old travel book about the East.
alone: Norman Douglas's Alone — essays and jottings from a solitary wanderer — sparkles with his mischievous wisdom. The South Wind author at his most personal. A connoisseur's companion. Mediterranean inns and bookish talk fill his solitary pages. His paradoxes provoke as much as they amuse.
anomalies-and-curiosities-of-medicine: A 1896 medical bestseller by doctors George Gould and Walter Pyle, collecting the strangest cases in the history of medicine. Human oddities, freak accidents, astonishing survivals, and surgical marvels fill its pages, drawn from centuries of journals. Half science and half sideshow, it fascinated Victorian readers and remains a jaw-dropping tour of what the human body can endure.
baby-mine: A popular play by Margaret Mayo about a wife who "borrows" a baby to win back her wandering husband, setting off a chain of comic mix-ups. A Broadway hit of 1910, it charmed audiences with its blend of farce and sentiment. This edition preserves a prime example of the light American comedy that packed theaters a century ago.
betty-zane: Zane Grey's 1903 first novel, based on his ancestress Elizabeth Zane, heroine of the siege of Fort Henry in 1782. Her famous run for gunpowder under Indian fire made her a frontier legend. Grey's tribute blends family history with rousing adventure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dunf: This 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia article on the Abbey of Dunfermline — burial place of Scottish kings, founded by St. Margaret — recounts its royal glory. Oswald Hunter-Blair gives its full story. A majestic reference on Scotland's Westminster. Bruce's heart, minus its crusade, rests in its choir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain: A 1913 entry on St. Augustine's, Canterbury — the apostle of England's own house. Rome's mission took root in Kent. George Cyprian Alston traces its story. Where English Christianity began. Its gate still greets pilgrims on the road to Canterbury. Ethelbert's tomb lies within its walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-bisho: A 1913 entry on Acacius of Caesarea — the Arian bishop who succeeded Eusebius. Cornelius Clifford tells his stormy story. Councils rose and fell around him. A prince of the losing side. His library preserved Origen's lost works. Jerome called him a one-eyed controversialist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-perse: A 1913 entry on Adam of Perseigne — the Cistercian abbot of mystical letters. Thomas Walsh praises his spiritual counsel. Kings and monks sought his advice. His letters breathe the cloister's peace. A director of souls in troubled times. His sermons on the Song of Songs are prized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonse-de-l: This 1913 reference article on Alphonse de Lamartine — the poet-statesman of France. Georges Bertrin weighs his fame and faith. His Méditations moved a generation. The 1848 republic heard his voice. France's singing statesman. His Jocelyn sang the priestly ideal. His fall was as swift as his rise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alsace-lorrai: This 1913 reference article on Alsace-Lorraine — the borderland's church story. Leo Ehrhard traces its sees through wars. France and Germany claimed its faith. Strasbourg's cathedral watched it all. A province between two empires. Its faith survived the changing flags. Its churches kept the French tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-stone: A 1913 entry on the altar stone — the consecrated slab with its relics. Augustin Schulte explains its necessity. Bishops seal the martyrs within. Missionaries carried such stones afar. The portable heart of the altar. Its cross is cut in the center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-wine: A 1913 entry on altar wine — the pure grape wine of the Mass. Augustin Schulte states the strict law. Only the vine's true juice suffices. Its care is the sacristan's trust. The chalice's worthy matter. Its cruet stands by the chalice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrogio-borg: This 1913 reference piece on Ambrogio Borgognone — the Lombard painter of quiet devotion. Augustus Van Cleef praises his altarpieces. His saints breathe a gentle piety. Milan's Certosa keeps his best. A master of the Lombard school. His frescoes glow in the Lombard chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce: A 1913 entry on Lindisfarne — the Holy Island of Aidan and Cuthbert. Columba Edmonds honors its golden age. The Gospels were painted in its scriptorium. Vikings reddened its shores with blood. England's holiest island. Its ruins crown the tidal island. Its mead hall is long silent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-ciccio: This 1913 reference article on Andrea Ciccione — the Neapolitan sculptor and architect. Marie Louise Handley praises his tombs. His work adorns the southern churches. The Renaissance bloomed in Naples. A master of the southern school. His portal graces the Naples churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-byrne: This 1913 reference piece on Andrew Byrne — the Bishop of Little Rock. Thomas Meehan sketches his pioneer rule. He built the Arkansas Church. The frontier tested his zeal. A bishop of the southwest. His cathedral crowns the Arkansas hills. His missions reached the frontier forts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiochus-of-: A 1913 entry on Antiochus of Palestine — a monk of the desert. Francis Grey notes his writings. The entry preserves his modest fame. The lavra kept his memory. A solitary of the Holy Land. His cell overlooked the Kidron valley. His writings survive in the collections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-elisa: This 1913 reference article on Dareste de la Chavanne — the historian of France. Louis Delamarre praises his nine volumes. His pages spanned the monarchy's tale. The Academy crowned his labors. A chronicler of the French past. His history fills the library shelves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assistant-at-: A 1913 entry on the Assistant at the Pontifical Throne — the honorary rank of bishops. William Fanning explains its stately use. The assistants stand near the pope. The title crowns long service. The papal court's episcopal guard. Its bearers assist at papal Masses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asylums-and-c: A 1913 entry on asylums and care for the insane — the Church's pioneering mercy. James Joseph Walsh honors its hospitals. St. Vincent's sons led the reform. The mad found shelter with the sisters. Charity's work among the afflicted. Its sisters still tend the afflicted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augusta-theod: A 1913 entry on Augusta Theodosia Drane — the Dominican historian. Edwin Burton honors her Christian Schools and Scholars. Her pen lit the medieval schools. Stone's mother-house knew her zeal. A nun among historians. Her Mozart biography is famed. Her order honors its historian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldassare-ca: A 1913 entry on Baldassare Castiglione — the author of The Courtier. Edoardo San Giovanni honors his urbane book. His perfect gentleman charmed Europe. Mantua's court was his school. The mirror of the Renaissance court. His book taught the courts of Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bayonne: This 1913 reference piece on Bayonne — the Basque diocese of the Adour. Georges Goyau gives its story. Its bishops serve the border flock. The Nive joins the Adour at its walls. A see of the Pyrenean edge. Its hams are famed through France.
